subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
passage: At school, Afreen took the long way to the chemistry lab so she wouldn't pass Jagdish's locker. Since his father died in June, he had called her almost every night, crying, talking till two. She listened every time. She felt his grief like a stone in her own chest, and lately she couldn't sleep even when he didn't call. This morning she'd fallen asleep in maths. When she saw Jagdish waiting at the lab door, she turned into the library instead, and stood between the shelves, hating herself. Ms Kurian, the librarian, looked up. 'Afreen? You look worn out.' Afreen's eyes filled. It all came out: the calls, the tiredness, the hiding. Ms Kurian listened, then said, 'You haven't done anything wrong. You've been carrying too much on your own.' She walked Afreen to the counsellor's room before lunch, and promised Jagdish would get support too.

qa.q: When did Jagdish's father die?
qa.a: In June.

qa.q: Why did Afreen hate herself between the shelves?
qa.a: Afreen cared deeply for Jagdish and felt guilty for avoiding him, but was too exhausted from carrying his grief to face him.

qa.q: What did Ms Kurian choose to do, and why was it important?
qa.a: Ms Kurian listened, told Afreen she had done nothing wrong, took her to the counsellor that same morning and promised support for Jagdish, so neither teen was left carrying the grief alone.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Afreen turns into the library?
qa.a: Jagdish, already grieving, may feel hurt and confused, wondering why Afreen, who listened every night, now seems to avoid him.

grounding: A teenager absorbs Jagdish's grief until, exhausted, she avoids him, and a librarian takes her to the counsellor.

subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
passage:
Dear Salma Ma'am,
You said at assembly we could write to you if something felt too heavy. This is Kiran from 10B.
My best friend's grandmother, who raised her, died last month. Since then she messages me every night, sometimes till 3 a.m. I read every message. I feel what she feels, as if it's happening to me. I've stopped sleeping properly, I cry on the bus, and my marks are falling.
And now I'm doing something awful. I leave her messages unread. Today I ate lunch in the washroom so she wouldn't find me. I love her. I just can't hold any more.
Can I see you today, before I go home? And please can someone help her too, because I can't be the only one.
Kiran
Reply, 11:20 a.m.: Kiran, come to my room at lunch today. You have done nothing wrong. We will make sure your friend gets support too. — Salma Ma'am

qa.q: Where did Kiran eat lunch today?
qa.a: In the washroom.

qa.q: What is Kiran feeling in "I love her. I just can't hold any more"?
qa.a: Kiran still cares deeply but is overwhelmed and exhausted from feeling the friend's grief, and feels guilty for pulling away.

qa.q: Why was writing to Salma Ma'am the right choice at this point?
qa.a: Kiran couldn't carry the grief alone, so bringing in the counsellor that same day gets help for both Kiran and the grieving friend.

qa.q: How might the grieving friend feel seeing the messages left unread?
qa.a: The friend may feel abandoned and even lonelier, not knowing Kiran is worn out rather than uncaring.

grounding: A teenager overwhelmed by a grieving friend's nightly messages starts avoiding her and writes to the counsellor for help.

subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
passage: Okay. So you want to know why I stopped sitting with Jasleen. I'm Alka, 11A. It's not because I don't care, Ma'am, I promise. When her parents split up in March, she told me everything. Every break, every night on the phone. The shouting, her father leaving, her mother crying in the kitchen. I felt all of it, like it was my house. I started waking at four with my heart racing. I snapped at my own mum. And then one day I just… couldn't. I saw her at the gate and walked the other way. I've done it for two weeks now. She looks at me like I slapped her. I feel horrible. I came to you today because I want to be her friend again, just not like this, all alone with it. The counsellor nodded. 'This isn't your fault, Alka. Today we'll find Jasleen more support, so you're not carrying it alone.'

qa.q: When did Jasleen's parents split up?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: Why did Alka walk the other way at the gate?
qa.a: Alka was so worn out from feeling all of Jasleen's pain that avoiding Jasleen felt like the only relief, even though it felt horrible.

qa.q: Why was coming to the counsellor a good choice for Alka?
qa.a: It gives Alka support and a way to stay Jasleen's friend without carrying everything alone, and the counsellor can help Jasleen too.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel during these two weeks?
qa.a: Jasleen probably feels hurt and confused, as if her closest support suddenly vanished at the hardest time.

grounding: A teenager drained by a friend's family crisis has been avoiding her, and tells the school counsellor she wants help to be a friend again.

subtype: Overwhelmed by a friend's crisis, then withdrawing [Actor]
passage:
I'm Nazia, Bidisha's classmate in Class 11. We share a bench, so I noticed it.
In September, Rimjhim's older brother was in a bad bike accident and was in hospital for weeks. Rimjhim is Bidisha's closest friend. For the first fortnight Bidisha was her rock. She stayed on the phone with her till late, went to the hospital after school, cried with her in the washroom.
Then Bidisha started coming in with dark circles, yawning through physics. She fell asleep in the library once. She stopped eating her tiffin.
By October, something flipped. When Rimjhim walked toward our bench, Bidisha suddenly needed to go to the staff room. Her phone buzzed and she turned it over without looking. I asked her if they'd fought. She said, "No. I just can't. I'm so tired." Her eyes filled up.
I don't know everything she was feeling. But she didn't look like someone who stopped caring.

qa.q: How long was Rimjhim's brother in hospital?
qa.a: He was in hospital for weeks.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when she said, "I just can't"?
qa.a: She was worn out and probably guilty; her filling eyes suggest she still cared about Rimjhim but had nothing left to give.

qa.q: What turning point could have changed how this went for Bidisha?
qa.a: If, when the tiredness began, Bidisha had told an adult and shared the support with others instead of carrying it alone, she might not have needed to pull away.

qa.q: How might Rimjhim feel when Bidisha suddenly leaves the bench?
qa.a: Rimjhim may feel confused and abandoned just when her family is struggling, not knowing that her friend is exhausted rather than uncaring.

grounding: It shows, through a classmate's eyes, a teenager who absorbs a friend's crisis, sleeps badly and then starts avoiding that friend out of exhaustion.

passage:
Tuesday. Tanvir called at eleven. His father had lost his job, and the family was giving up the flat and moving back to the village after his exams. He cried for two hours. Sudha lay under her blanket listening, her own throat aching, and only slept after one.
Saturday. Sudha had called Tanvir every night that week. She skipped tuition because her head was pounding. At nine her phone lit up: "You there?" She stared at it, then put it face down under her pillow and pretended to be asleep. Her heart was thumping with guilt.
Next Thursday. In the school corridor, Tanvir waved at her from the water cooler. Sudha turned into the girls' washroom and stood by the sink, breathing fast. She wanted to help him. She also wanted, more than anything, to not hear one more sad thing.

qa.q: Where did Tanvir wave at Sudha from?
qa.a: From the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Sudha's thumping heart on Saturday reveal about her?
qa.a: It reveals she felt guilty for ignoring Tanvir; she still cared, but she was too exhausted to answer.

qa.q: At which point could Sudha have made a different choice, and what might have helped?
qa.a: On Saturday, instead of hiding the phone, Sudha could have told Tanvir she needed rest and suggested he also talk to another friend or an adult, so the weight was shared.

qa.q: How might Tanvir experience Sudha turning into the washroom?
qa.a: He might feel rejected and even more alone, just when his family is losing their home, without knowing Sudha is worn out rather than uncaring.

grounding: It shows a teenager who takes in a friend's grief night after night, sleeps badly and then starts avoiding the friend out of exhaustion.
